words.definition: A way of life that involves a lot of sitting and very little physical activity.
words.example: The shift towards office-based work has led to increasingly sedentary lifestyles, contributing to obesity and heart disease.
collocations: the risks of a sedentary lifestyle

words.definition: Intended to stop an illness or problem from happening, rather than treating it afterwards.
words.example: Investing in preventive healthcare, such as vaccination and screening, is far more cost-effective than treating advanced disease.

words.definition: The condition of being so overweight that it is dangerous to your health.
words.example: Childhood obesity has reached epidemic proportions in many high-income countries.

words.definition: The average number of years that a person is expected to live.
words.example: Improvements in sanitation and nutrition have dramatically increased life expectancy over the past century.

words.definition: Pressure on a system, organisation or person caused by having too much to deal with.
words.example: An ageing population is placing enormous strain on public health services and the staff who run them.

words.definition: Describing an illness or problem that lasts for a long time or keeps coming back.
words.example: Chronic conditions such as diabetes and heart disease now account for the majority of healthcare spending.

words.definition: The state of being healthy, comfortable and happy, both physically and mentally.
words.example: Employers are increasingly recognising that staff well-being has a direct impact on productivity.

words.definition: Strong feelings of shame or disapproval that society attaches to a particular condition or group.
words.example: Despite growing awareness, a stigma still surrounds mental illness, discouraging many people from seeking help.

words.definition: Easily affected or harmed by something, such as a disease.
words.example: Elderly people are particularly susceptible to respiratory infections during the winter months.
Prolonged exposure to air pollution can be detrimental to both physical and cognitive health.

words.definition: A system in which every citizen can receive medical treatment, regardless of their income.
words.example: Supporters of universal healthcare argue that access to treatment should never depend on one's ability to pay.

words.definition: To stop something harmful, such as a disease, from spreading or becoming worse.
words.example: Early testing and contact tracing proved crucial in containing the spread of the virus.

words.definition: Food that has been changed by industrial methods, often with added salt, sugar, fat or preservatives.
words.example: Heavily processed food has been linked to a higher risk of heart disease and type 2 diabetes.

words.definition: To make pain, suffering or a problem less severe.
words.example: Expanding community clinics could help alleviate pressure on overcrowded hospital emergency departments.

words.definition: Dealing with the whole person or situation, including mind, body and lifestyle, rather than just one part.
words.example: A more holistic approach to healthcare would address patients' diet, sleep and stress levels as well as their symptoms.

words.definition: The process of protecting people from a disease, usually by giving them a vaccine.
words.example: Falling immunisation rates have allowed diseases such as measles to return in several European countries.
